Museum of Modern Art. MoMA opened in 1929 and established the canonical taste for twentieth-century modernism and contemporary practice. Its collection defines what modern art means: painting, sculpture, photography, film, and design from Impressionism onward. Founded by Abby Aldrich Rockefeller and others, MoMA has been located in Midtown Manhattan since 1939, with multiple expansions through the nineteen-eighties and two-thousands. The museum holds the world's most influential collection of twentieth-century painting and sculpture, including Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and works by Matisse, Pollock, and Rothko. A particular strength is its pioneering role in presenting photography, film, and graphic design as fine art. MoMA's photography collection is canonical and world-class, establishing photography as a museum-worthy medium equal to painting. The building by Philip Goodwin and Edward Durrell Stone, completed in 1939, became a modernist landmark itself. Recent expansions by Diller Scofidio and Renfro were completed in 2019. What distinguishes MoMA from purely historical collections is its emphasis on living artists and contemporary practice, which sets it apart from other institutions. It hosts provocative and sometimes controversial exhibitions that keep the conversation about modern art vital and urgent. The museum owns works by nearly every major modernist and contemporary artist, and its holdings include globally recognizable masterpieces like Van Gogh's Starry Night and Salvador Dalí's The Persistence of Memory. These works shaped the American canon of Action Painting and Color Field abstraction for decades.
